concepts.title: Concluding Remarks

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: In this chapter we have reviewed some of the key components of a system trained to estimate depth from single images.
concepts.content: In this chapter we have reviewed some of the key components of a system trained to estimate depth from single images. The methods are similar to other regression problems and most of the challenge consists of identifying how to collect the data needed for training. Supervised methods are more reliable than unsupervised methods for now. Unsupervised methods rely on learning to estimate depth using the constraints present between camera motion, 3D, and photometric consistency. Unsupervised learning allows a system to learn from a very diverse set of data (as the only thing needed is video captured by a moving camera), and to adapt to new environments where ground truth supervision is not available.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding depth estimation methods helps in building systems that can infer 3D structure from images, especially when ground truth data is scarce.

- Supervised methods are currently more reliable than unsupervised ones.
- Unsupervised learning leverages camera motion and photometric consistency constraints.

concepts.title: Monocular Depth Cues

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Monocular depth cues are image features used by the human visual system to interpret the 3D structure of a picture.
concepts.content:
Before delving into the subject of this chapter, let's quickly review some of the image features that are used by the human visual system to interpret the 3D structure of a picture.

For a greater understanding of depth cues, take an art class.

**Shading** refers to the changes in image intensity produced by changes in surface orientation. The amount of light reflected in the direction of the viewer by a surface illuminated by a directional light source is a function of the surface albedo, the light intensity, and the relative angle between the light direction and the surface normal orientation, as discussed in the section on light interacting with surfaces. **Shape from shading** studies how to recover shape by inverting the rendering equations.

Another source of 3D information is **texture gradients**. Since distant things appear smaller than closer things, by measuring the relative size between textural elements that appear in different image regions, we can get a coarse estimate of the 3D scene structure (see figure aerial perspective [a]). Many methods using texture gradient cues have been proposed over time.

Another source of information about the 3D scene structure is shadows and interreflections. An example of how interreflections can inform us about the location of a ball was seen in the section on looking at images. The use of shadows and interreflections by the human visual system has been the focus of many studies. There are also computational approaches that use shadows and interreflections to recover 3D.

When looking at large landscapes, like a mountain range, mountains that are far away have lower contrast due to dispersion by the atmosphere (see figure aerial perspective [b]). This effect gets accentuated when there is fog. Therefore, contrast can be used as a cue to infer relative distances between objects. This depth cue is called **aerial perspective** or atmospheric perspective. One example using haze to infer depth is in Kaiming 2009.

[FIGURE:74c32638e485d003 | A close-up photograph of a textured metal surface with a repeating grid of small, square-based pyramidal bumps. The perspective view shows the bumps receding into the distance, illustrating how...]

[FIGURE:52838648eb2a6dee | A photograph of a deep mountain valley illustrating aerial perspective. The foreground mountains are dark green and high contrast, while the distant mountain peaks appear lighter, bluer, and lower in...]

Fig (a) This image contains multiple 3D cues: shading effects (bump shapes), texture gradients (relative size between bumps), and linear perspective (due to the regular arrangement of the bumps). (b) Aerial perspective. Objects far in the background have lower contrast than objects closer to the camera.

Depth can also be estimated by detecting **familiar objects** with known sizes. One example is people detection. Objects with known sizes can be used to estimate absolute depth while many of the cues that we discussed before can only give relative depth measurements. One example of using object sizes to reason about 3D geometry is Hoiem 2008.

And finally, **linear perspective** provides strong cues for 3D reconstruction as studied earlier.
concepts.motivation_md: Monocular depth cues help humans and algorithms interpret 3D structure from 2D images, enabling depth perception and scene understanding from a single viewpoint.
concepts.recap_md:
- Monocular depth cues include shading, texture gradients, shadows, and aerial perspective.
- Familiar objects with known sizes help estimate absolute depth.
- Linear perspective provides strong 3D reconstruction cues.

concepts.title: Translating the depth map into a point cloud
aliases: depth map to point cloud conversion

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud is: $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$.
concepts.content:
Using homogeneous coordinates, the equation translating a depth map into a 3D point cloud is (for each pixel):
$$\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$$
where $\mathbf{p}$ are the pixel coordinates of a point, $z(\mathbf{p})$ is the depth measured at that location, and $\mathbf{P}$ are the final 3D point coordinates. In heterogeneous coordinates, and making the pixel locations explicit, equation (@eq-3dcloudpointfromz) can be rewritten as:
$$\begin{aligned}
    X[n,m] &= \left( n-c_x \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Y[n,m] &= \left( m-c_y \right) \frac{z[n,m]}{a} \\
    Z[n,m] &= z[n,m] 
\end{aligned}$$
where $a$, $c_x$ and $c_y$ are the intrinsic camera parameters (in pixel units). This writing shows that the 3D point coordinates are three images $X[n,m]$, $Y[n,m]$, and $Z[n,m]$ with the same size as the input image.

![Translating the depth map into a point cloud. This requires a calibrated camera (i.e., knowing the intrinsic camera parameters). The sketch shows how one pixel $(n,m)$ is mapped into a 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, by using the depth, $z[n,m]$, at that location. Colored lines are parallel to the respective axis direction in the camera coordinates system.](figures/learning_3d/from_depthmap_2_pointcloud.png){width="100%" #fig-kinect2}
concepts.motivation_md: Converting depth maps to 3D point clouds allows reconstruction of the 3D scene geometry from 2D images using camera calibration parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth maps can be converted to 3D point clouds using camera intrinsics.
- Equation: $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$.
- Coordinates $X[n,m], Y[n,m], Z[n,m]$ correspond to 3D points per pixel.

concepts.title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Learning-based methods can extract and combine many cues from images to provide depth estimates from a single image.
concepts.content: Previous computer vision approaches for 3D reconstruction from single images focused on developing the formulation to extract depth using one or few of the cues we discussed in the previous section, and can only be applied to a restricted set of images. Learning-based methods instead have the potential to learn to extract many cues from images, decide which cues are more relevant in each case, and combine them to provide depth estimates. There were a number of early models that applied learning for recovering 3D scene structure @Saxena2008, @Derek2005 but in this chapter we will focus on methods using deep learning although the approaches described here are independent of the particular learning architecture used.
concepts.motivation_md: Learning-based methods enable depth estimation from single images by combining multiple cues, overcoming limitations of traditional cue-specific approaches.
concepts.recap_md:
- Traditional methods use limited cues for depth estimation.
- Learning-based methods can combine multiple cues.
- Deep learning is the focus for modern depth estimation.

concepts.title: Depth estimation as a pixelwise regression problem

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Depth estimation becomes a pixelwise regression problem using a learnable function $h_\theta$.
concepts.content:
In the supervised setting we will assume that we have a training set that contains $N$ images, $\ell^{(i)} [n,m]$, and their associated depth maps, $z^{(i)} [n,m]$. In this formulation, depth estimation becomes a pixelwise regression problem. Usually $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}$ and $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$ are images of the same size. Our goal is to estimate depth at each pixel, $\hat{z}^{(i)}[n,m]$, from a single image using a learnable function, $h_\theta$:
$$\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)} = h_\theta \left( \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)} \right)$$
where the parameters $\theta$ are learned by minimizing the loss over a training set:
$$\theta^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\theta} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{z}^{(i)} \right)$$
concepts.motivation_md: Formulating depth estimation as pixelwise regression allows learning a function to predict depth from image pixels directly.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth estimation is formulated as pixelwise regression.
- Learnable function $h_\theta$ maps images to depth maps.
- Parameters $\theta$ are optimized by minimizing loss on training data.

concepts.title: Collecting Training Data

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Efficient and scalable data collection strategies are crucial for supervised depth estimation.
concepts.content:
Coming up with efficient and scalable data collection strategies is crucial in this task. Several methods for supervised learning from single images differ mostly on how they collect the data. This simplest data capture method is using a depth sensor such as an RGB-D camera or a light detection and ranging (LiDAR) device.

LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) is a device that calculates distances by measuring the time taken for emitted light to return after reflecting off a surface (time of flight). A LiDAR produces a range image by scanning multiple directions. The output is a point cloud.

Two examples of datasets are the NYUv2 dataset @SilbermanECCV12, captured using a handheld Microsoft Kinect sensor while walking indoors, and the KITTI dataset @Geiger2013, collected from a moving vehicle with a LiDAR scan.

Other methods consist of using stereo pairs for training @Xian2018 or multiview geometry methods that provide more accurate 3D estimates. MegaDepth @MegaDepthLi18 uses scenes captured with multiple cameras to get good 3D reconstructions using structure from motion techniques. This allows creating a dataset of images and associated depth maps that can be used to train depth from single image methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Collecting diverse and accurate training data is essential for supervised learning methods to estimate depth from single images effectively.

concepts.one_liner: One simple loss is the L2 loss between the estimated depth, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ and the ground truth depth, $\mathbf{z}$.
concepts.content:
Once we have a dataset, the next steps consist in using an appropriate loss to optimize the parameters of the depth estimator. One simple loss is the L2 loss between the estimated depth, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ and the ground truth depth, $\mathbf{z}$. The loss is defined as:

$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{z} \right) =  \sum_{n,m} \left( \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m] \right) ^2$$
concepts.motivation_md: The L2 loss provides a straightforward way to measure and minimize the difference between estimated and true depth values, enabling optimization of depth estimation models.
concepts.recap_md:
- The L2 loss measures squared differences between estimated and ground truth depth.
- It sums over all pixel locations $(n,m)$.
- Used to optimize depth estimator parameters.

concepts.title: scale-invariant loss

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Supervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The scale-invariant loss addresses this by eliminating the global scale factor from the calculation.
concepts.content:
The **scale-invariant loss** addresses the problem of global scale factor ambiguity by eliminating it from the calculation:

$$\mathcal{L} \left( \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{z} \right) =  \sum_{n,m} \left( \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m] - \alpha\right) ^2$$

where $\alpha = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{n,m} \hat{z}[n,m] - z[n,m]$. This loss compares the estimated and ground truth depth at each pixel independently.

To achieve a more globally consistent reconstruction, one can also introduce depth derivatives into the loss, although ground truth derivatives might be noisy depending on how the depth has been collected.

Optimizing depth reconstruction might overemphasize errors for points with large depth values. One way to mitigate this is to optimize the reconstruction of the log of the depth, $\log \left( z[n,m] \right)$, or the disparity, which corresponds to the inverse of the depth, $1/z[n,m]$.

A more complete set of losses are reviewed in @Ranftl2021, @Ranftl2022.
concepts.motivation_md: Depth estimation errors can be biased by global scale and large depth values; the scale-invariant loss removes global scale effects and can incorporate derivatives to improve consistency.
concepts.recap_md:
- Scale-invariant loss removes global scale factor $\alpha$ from depth error.
- It compares estimated and ground truth depth pixel-wise.
- Log-depth or disparity can mitigate errors from large depth values.

concepts.title: Unsupervised learning of depth and camera motion by image reconstruction

concepts.one_liner: As a camera moves in the world, the pixel values between two images captured at two different time instants are related by the 3D scene structure and the relative camera motion between the two frames.
concepts.content:
A different, and likely simpler, approach to learning depth without supervision is to use motion and temporal consistency as a supervisory signal @Tinghui2017. As a camera moves in the world, the pixel values between two images captured at two different time instants are related by the 3D scene structure and the relative camera motion between the two frames.

Therefore, we can formulate the problem as an image prediction problem. Let's say we have a function $f_1$ that can estimate depth from a single image, and a function $f_2$ that takes as input two frames, $\boldsymbol\ell_1$ and $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, and estimates the relative camera positions (the rotation and translation matrices, $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{T}$) between the two frames, as shown in @fig-unsupervised_depth_system:

$$\begin{aligned}
\hat{\mathbf{z}} &= f_1(\boldsymbol\ell) \\
\left[ \hat{\mathbf{R}},\hat{\mathbf{T}} \right] &= f_2(\boldsymbol\ell_1,\boldsymbol\ell_2)
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Image warping for depth and camera motion estimation

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: Warping is a deterministic function that takes as input a reference frame, the depth map, and the relative camera motion matrices and outputs an image.
concepts.content:
Warping is a deterministic function ($f_3$ in @fig-unsupervised_depth_system) that takes as input a reference frame, the depth map, and the relative camera motion matrices and outputs an image:

$$\boldsymbol\ell_{1 \rightarrow 2} =  
f_3(\boldsymbol\ell_1, \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{T})$$

The function $f_3$ is built with the tools we have studied in the previous chapters. In section @sec-image_wrapping we described the procedure for warping an image using backward warping. Here we will use the same procedure.

The goal is to warp a **reference frame** into a **target frame**. We want to look over all pixel locations, $\mathbf{x}$, over the target frame $\boldsymbol\ell_2$, and compute the corresponding location on the reference frame $\boldsymbol\ell_1$. For each pixel on the target frame, we will follow the next steps (see @fig-geometry_reconstruction for the geometric interpretation of all the steps):

-   Express the image coordinates of the pixel in the target frame in homogeneous coordinates, $\mathbf{p}$.

-   Given the depth at that location, recover the 3D world coordinates of the target point, $\mathbf{P}$. To do this we will use the intrinsic camera matrix, assumed to be known, and the depth at that point: $\mathbf{P} = z(\mathbf{p}) \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{p}$. As we do not have access to ground truth depth, we will use the function $f_1$ to estimate depth: $\hat{\mathbf{z}} = f_1(\boldsymbol\ell_2)$. The coordinates of the point $\mathbf{P}$ are expressed with respect to the camera coordinates of $\boldsymbol\ell_2$.

-   We now use the camera rotation and translation matrices to change the camera coordinates to the coordinates defined by the reference frame, $\boldsymbol\ell_1$. This is done as $\mathbf{P}' = \mathbf{M}\mathbf{P}$ where the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ contains the translation and rotation matrices.

-   Finally, we project the point $\mathbf{P}'$ into the image coordinates of the reference frame $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{P}'$.

-   The resulting coordinates $\mathbf{p}'$ are translated back into heterogeneous coordinates.

(see figure: Geometry between two images captured by a moving camera. The coordinates of corresponding points between the two frames are constrained by the 3D world coordinates of the point the relative camera...)
concepts.motivation_md: Image warping uses estimated depth and camera motion to reconstruct one frame from another, enabling unsupervised learning by comparing reconstructed and actual images.

- Warping function $f_3$ maps a reference frame to a target frame using depth and camera motion.
- Steps include coordinate transformation from target to reference frame.
- Uses intrinsic camera matrix and estimated depth for 3D point recovery.

concepts.title: Image reconstruction loss for unsupervised depth learning

position.chapter_title: Learning to Estimate Depth from a Single Image
position.section_title: Unsupervised Methods for Depth from a Single Image

concepts.one_liner: The loss is computed only over the valid set of pixels using a mask that excludes pixels outside the visible part of the reference frame.
concepts.content:
The image reconstruction loss for unsupervised depth learning is defined as:

$$\mathcal{L} =  \sum_{n,m} v\left(n,m \right) \left( \ell_{1 \rightarrow 2}[n,m] - \ell_{2}[n,m] \right) ^2$$

As only the pixels with coordinates $\mathbf{p}'$ inside the image can be reconstructed by warping, we compute the loss only over the valid set of pixels. This is done using the mask $v\left(n,m \right)$, which is 1 for valid pixels and 0 for pixels that lie outside the visible part of the reference frame. The mask could also exclude pixels that fall in moving objects as those will have displacements that cannot be predicted by the motion of the camera alone.
concepts.motivation_md: Using a mask to compute the reconstruction loss only over valid pixels ensures accurate training by ignoring pixels that cannot be reconstructed or belong to moving objects.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reconstruction loss measures squared difference between warped and target images.
- Mask $v(n,m)$ selects valid pixels inside the reference frame.
- Mask can exclude moving objects with unpredictable motion.

concepts.one_liner: Not all camera motions provide enough information to learn about the 3D world structure.
concepts.content: Not all camera motions provide enough information to learn about the 3D world structure. As we discussed in chapter @sec-homography, if all the videos contain only sequences captured by a rotating camera, the points are related by a homography regardless of the 3D structure. Therefore, to learn depth from single images, we need to have complex camera motions inside environments with rich 3D structure.
concepts.motivation_md: Learning depth from single images requires diverse camera motions and rich 3D environments to provide sufficient geometric information.
concepts.recap_md:
- Simple camera motions like pure rotation yield homographies independent of 3D structure.
- Complex camera motions are necessary to learn depth.
- Environments must have rich 3D structure for effective learning.
